articleTitle: Fluoride Removal from Calcium-Rich Mine Water by Steel Slag Adsorption
abstract: The objective of this work was to design a process to remove fluoride from a mining wastewater stream and reduce the concentrations of fluoride below the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) secondary drinking water standard of 2 mg/L fluoride. The effectiveness of electric arc furnace (EAF) steel slag as a method for fluoride removal was investigated. The synthetic mine water contained a range of ortho-phosphates, 1.7 g/L gypsum, and 22.1 mg/L sodium fluoride. Batch testing using glass beakers to test various conditions of the slag were conducted. Two columns in series filled with EAF slag were bottom fed with the synthetic mining water for continuous testing. The best fluoride removal occurred when the phosphates to sulfates ratio was 3:1, at 89.6% removed. Fluoride concentrations were tested using a fluoride ion selective electrode (ISE). The best results occurred at a neutral to slightly basic pH. From testing, it was concluded there are three reaction mechanisms removing the fluoride. The main mechanism through the formation of fluorapatite, Ca<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sub>(PO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sub>)<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>F. The second mechanism uses competitive adsorption between hydroxides and metal ions in solution, formed from the steel slag, to form a flocculant with the fluoride ion. The third happens from the formation of calcium fluoride. The desorption of fluoride from the surface of the slag was explored, but could not be tested due to laboratory restrictions.

articleTitle: Wireless soil moisture sensor networks for agriculture
abstract: Over 60% of agricultural water is wasted due to inefficient irrigation that results from a lack of crop and soil monitoring. Most solutions to this problem are either too expensive for small farmers or lack feasibility of implementation in large-scale commercial farms. A soil moisture wireless sensor network is a promising solution, which can be readily deployed in small, as well as commercial farms, and has been proven to increase irrigation efficiency. However, these systems are generally expensive or are not thoroughly designed for all situations. We propose and test a Wireless Soil Moisture Sensor Network for Agriculture as a system of interconnected, self-sufficient, solar-powered sensor nodes and centralized gateways. Thus, providing farmers with real-time information of soil-moisture, soil-temperature, relative humidity, and weather. Six nodes and one gateway were deployed and tested for four months, and have proven to be reliable and self-sufficient, all while continuing to transmit sensor data, which is successfully logged by the centralized gateway onto a website capable of time-based graphical analysis. The system has also shown to be easily adaptable, as changes and modifications were made to the network. In addition, the proposed system is comprehensive, cost-effective, and scalable. It can be deployed in both commercial and small farms so that farmers can make informed decisions on irrigation and crop management, which consequently increases irrigation efficiency and agricultural productivity.

articleTitle: Effects of Phase Change Material on Solar Panel Power Output
abstract: This report outlines a cost-effective, self-sustaining, and environmentally responsible solution of passive cooling technologies in conjunction with a photovoltaic solar panel system to improve power output in response to Task 1 for the WERC Environmental Design Contest. PCMs have been used in many different practices to modulate temperatures both hot and cold. The PCM utilized is the proprietary PureTemp© 37X, with a phase change that occurs at 37°C. This was hypothesized to keep the solar panel at or below the nominal operating temperature of 45°C and improve efficiency. Testing showed that overall efficiency was improved with the addition of PureTemp© 37X to the rear side of the solar panel. The largest average improvement in power output when compared to the control was 2.9% at the maximum thickness (5.5cm), while the thinnest box (2.5 cm) had an average power output improvement of 0.79%. Assuming all the energy from the surface of the solar panels entered the PCM, with standard conditions of 21.5°C, 3.79 m/s wind speed, solar irradiance of 5890 W-hr/m2, the solar panel would remain below the nominal operating temperature for approximately 3 to 4 hours. Cost analysis based on the National Renewable Energy Laboratory Utility PV 2018 Cost Model predicts that PV panels must have an efficiency increase of 14.9% with PCM attachment, compared to a control panel, to be financially reasonable.

Acid Rock Drainage (ARD) is a growing environmental problem and is characterized by acidic, heavy metal-laden water. Here we consider the use of algae to remediate ARD and heavy metal pollution. Algae species candidates that remediate heavy metals from impacted waters with a 90% efficiency while sustaining highly acidic, metal-laden conditions were explored. The following phycoremediation candidates were selected, cultivated, and intended to be tested for their metal-sorption capacity and ideal operational conditions: Spirulina platensis, Cladophora glomerata, a sample from mine water, and a sample local to New Orleans, Louisiana. Due to the unexpected remote-only working constraints, only the local sample was tested for its metal removal efficiency on synthetic multi-metal mine water and at only one operational condition: contact time. Optimum contact times varied upon the different metals: 75 minutes (Al), 15 minutes (As), 60 minutes (Cu), and 30 minutes (Fe, Mn, and Zn).After practicing phycoremediation in the lab, a full-scale system for mass-cultivation of algae and treatment of acid rock drainage with an influent flow rate of 10 GPM was designed. An ORWP was selected for the mass-cultivation of the algae and the required pond area was determined to be 700 m<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. For the treatment system, a sequencing batch reactor (SBR) design was selected with three batch reactors each with a volume of 1500 gallons to account for a 10 GPM flow per tank per cycle. To separate the biomass from the treated mine water, a concurrent inclined settling system and flocculant was chosen. A mass balance was applied to the system to find the flow of biomass exiting and the amount of truckloads per year required for disposal of the biomass. From a cost analysis, the estimated capital and annual costs of a full-scale ARD treatment phycoremediation system is estimated to be $361,943 and $244,821/year, respectively.
